summary:
The question for the last two weeks is not how to raise national turnout. It is how to raise change-bloc turnout more than Netanyahu-bloc (NB) turnout without waking the NB's larger pool of low-propensity voters.

1. GOTV that scales. Social-pressure mail still works in high-salience elections, but far less: about 0.7 pp across 1.96 million voters (D11-F01), against 8.1 pp in the low-salience original (D3-F05). It needs individual vote histories, which Israeli campaigns do not lawfully hold (D5-F25), so it cannot be used as designed. What carries over is the framing: say that turnout is high and never lament low turnout (D11-F03). Descriptive norms alone add little (D11-F04), and wording tricks do not scale (D11-F05). Impersonal digital contact barely moves turnout. An $8.9M, 2-million-person social-ad programme had zero average effect (D11-F08). A platform-wide election-day prompt with friends' faces added 0.24 pp, and spillover to close friends doubled it (D11-F06). The only scalable channel with large effects is relational. Supervised 'captains' each mobilising about ten named friends raised turnout 13 pp in a low-salience pilot (D11-F09; D3-F12). After discounting for salience and for 75-80% baselines, budget 1-8 pp (central 3) per assigned friend.

2. Polls and expectations. Telling individuals the race is close does not move them (at most 0.8 pp; D11-F10, D11-F11). Published close polls do raise aggregate turnout: about 1.2 pp for a poll 7.65 points closer, mostly on the trailing side (D11-F12). Certainty demobilises. Exit-poll knowledge cut turnout by about 11 pp and fed bandwagon voting (D11-F13), and probability forecasts inflate perceived certainty (D11-F15). Lab work disputes the direction (D11-F16). Poll momentum shifts votes mainly within blocs (D11-F17, D11-F18). Israel's poll blackout runs from the end of Friday 23 October to the close of polls (D11-F14), the window of Likud's 2015 late surge (D11-F30).

3. Counter-mobilisation. Negative partisanship and affective polarisation raise turnout, by about 9 pp in European PR systems (D11-F19, D11-F20), and anger mobilises (D11-F21). Negativity does not depress turnout on average (D11-F22). It demobilises only voters already committed to the candidate under attack (D11-F23). Official Israeli results show how large opponent responses can be:
- After Likud's 2019 camera campaign, Arab-list votes rose 39.5% while total votes rose 2.9% (D11-F27).
- Between September 2019 and March 2020, Likud added 239,000 votes (D11-F28).
- In 2022, Haredi lists grew 19% and the right 8%, while change-camp lists fell 0.8% (D11-F29).
Likud fights visible opposition-aligned mobilisation in the courts and in its messaging (D11-F33).

The asymmetry. On the atlas's 2026 projection (D11-F34):
- A 1-point turnout rise across NB-leaning segments nets about 10,800 votes for the NB.
- The same rise across change-leaning Jewish segments nets about 6,800 for the change bloc.
- A uniform national rise nets about 3,100 for the NB.
A realistic change-bloc programme yields 745-2,046 net vote-equivalents, so NB counter-mobilisation of only 0.07-0.19 pp would cancel it. The change bloc leads on enthusiasm (80% vs 72% certain to vote; D6-F38), but its strongholds are near their ceiling and the unmobilised reservoir sits on the NB side (D5-F16, D5-F17). Haredi turnout is the NB's weak flank this year (D11-F31, D11-F32).

Implications for 13-27 October:
(a) Mobilise through closed channels: relational captains on WhatsApp, supporter lists and household spillover, not broadcast.
(b) Use a high-turnout norm and an 'every vote to 61' frame. Never publicise surges in change strongholds or claim the race is decided. Present forecasts in seats, not win probabilities.
(c) Aim anger at the government's record (October 7, the draft) and deliver it to the bloc's own base. Avoid content that NB groups would read as a threat to their group.
(d) Run no visible, foreign-funded or transport-heavy operations, and clear everything with election counsel.
(e) Prepare a protocol for the Central Elections Committee's intraday polling-station turnout releases: respond inside the bloc's own networks, never with a public counter-'gevalt' (alarm) campaign.
(f) Do not hand Haredi leaders a mobilising threat. Keep the draft argument out of Haredi media spaces.

findings.topic: Social-pressure mail at scale, high salience
findings.claim: A nonpartisan campaign randomly mailed 'Self' social-pressure mailers to 1.96 million registered voters in 17 states before the 2014 US midterms. Each mailer showed the recipient's own past turnout and compared it with the median registrant in their state. The mailer raised validated turnout, but by about a tenth of the effect seen in the original low-salience Michigan study. Effects were broadly consistent across states and somewhat larger where the race was less salient.
findings.quant: ITT +0.7 pp (+2.2% relative to baseline); N about 1.96 million; 17 states; 2014 general election. Compare the 2006 Michigan primary 'Neighbors' mailer, +8.1 pp (D3-F05).
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Gregory A. Huber; Albert H. Fang; Andrew Gooch
findings.title: The Generalizability of Social Pressure Effects on Turnout Across High-Salience Electoral Contexts: Field Experimental Evidence From 1.96 Million Citizens in 17 States
findings.relevance: Social pressure survives scale and salience, but at well under 1 pp. Its key ingredient, an individual vote history, is not available to Israeli campaigns: parties receive the voter register (D6-F24), which as far as we could establish carries no individual turnout history, and the High Court has barred polling-station representatives from reporting which identifiable voters have voted (D5-F25). As designed it cannot be deployed in 2026. Only the norm-based framing transfers (D11-F03).

findings.topic: Social pressure in a hotly contested election
findings.claim: The 'Neighbors' mailer, which discloses the recipient's and their neighbours' past turnout, was re-tested during the heavily contested 2012 Wisconsin recall election. The effect was smaller than in the low-salience original but still sizable, and largest among low-propensity voters. Turnout of recipients was also higher in the presidential election months later. Partisan and nonpartisan wording worked equally well, and recipients were not targeted more often by later campaigns.
findings.quant: Point estimate not extracted (article paywalled); the abstract describes the effect as smaller than the low-salience 8.1 pp (D3-F05) but sizable, and concentrated among low-propensity voters. Partisan and nonpartisan versions had similar immediate and downstream effects.
findings.authors: Todd Rogers; Donald P. Green; John Ternovski; Carolina Ferrerosa Young
findings.title: Social pressure and voting: A field experiment conducted in a high-salience election
findings.relevance: A partisan sender does not blunt social pressure. In Israel the binding constraint is data, not who signs the message. The lasting habit effect (see D3-F30) means mobilising first-time and occasional change voters in 2026 has value beyond this election.

findings.topic: Descriptive norms: 'everybody is voting'
findings.claim: Two GOTV script experiments (New Jersey 2005, California 2006) found that messages stressing high expected turnout motivated voters more than messages stressing low turnout. The effect appeared mainly among infrequent and occasional voters. The authors warn that politicians and media who lament low participation may depress turnout.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted. The outcome was stated intention to vote, not validated turnout; the effect was concentrated among occasional voters.
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Todd Rogers
findings.title: Descriptive Social Norms and Motivation to Vote: Everybody's Voting and So Should You
findings.relevance: Change-bloc copy should say 'record turnout, everyone around you is voting', not 'our voters are staying home'. Likud's 'gevalt' format ('our people are staying home, the other side is voting in droves') pairs a low-turnout norm with an outgroup threat. Its apparent success (D11-F30) depends on the threat component, which the change bloc should not copy (D11-F27, D11-F34).

findings.topic: Descriptive norms alone vs vote-history pressure
findings.claim: A field experiment that varied the content of social-pressure mail found that showing recipients their own and their neighbours' vote histories made mail more effective. Individual vote history was the key ingredient. Less specific turnout information, such as community-wide rates, had weaker effects, and descriptive-norm appeals alone did little to raise turnout.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted; the direction of the effects comes from the abstract.
findings.authors: Costas Panagopoulos; Christopher W. Larimer; Meghan Condon
findings.title: Social Pressure, Descriptive Norms, and Voter Mobilization
findings.relevance: High-turnout framing is a cheap 'do no harm' rule, not a turnout engine. Without vote histories, an Israeli campaign can only apply personal accountability through people who know the voter: friends, family and captains (D11-F09, D3-F12).

findings.topic: Identity-wording 'hacks' do not scale
findings.claim: An early small study claimed that calling people 'voters' (noun) rather than asking them 'to vote' (verb) raised turnout by 11-14 points. A large preregistered replication in the 2016 US presidential election, including competitive states, found no effect. An earlier large replication in 2015 (Political Psychology, online 2017; doi:10.1111/pops.12446) had also found none.
findings.quant: Original claim +11 to +14 pp from two small experiments; large-scale replications: no detectable effect (point estimates not extracted).
findings.authors: Alan S. Gerber; Gregory A. Huber; Albert H. Fang
findings.title: Voting behavior is unaffected by subtle linguistic cues: Evidence from a psychologically authentic replication
findings.relevance: The budget should go to contacts, not to copywriting 'nudges'. Any vendor promising large turnout gains from message wording alone should be asked for a randomised test.

findings.topic: Election-day social-media reminder at scale
findings.claim: Facebook replicated its 2010 experiment on US election day 2012, showing an 'I voted' banner and friends' faces to about 15 million users matched to voter files. Validated turnout rose despite the high salience of a presidential election. Close friends of recipients also voted more, and the indirect effect on friends was estimated at about twice the direct effect.
findings.quant: ITT +0.24 pp (95% CI 0.03-0.44; 74.08% treated vs 73.91% untreated), controlling for 2010 vote. Banner alone or feed alone: n.s. About 90,000 direct plus 180,000 friend votes, roughly 270,000 in total. 15,060,897 matched users in 13 states. 2010 per-person effect about 0.40 pp; see Bond et al. 2012 (D3-F11).
findings.authors: Jason J. Jones; Robert M. Bond; Eytan Bakshy; Dean Eckles; James H. Fowler
findings.title: Social influence and political mobilization: Further evidence from a randomized experiment in the 2012 U.S. presidential election
findings.relevance: An election-day reminder with social proof works a little, and most of its value travels through close ties. The change bloc cannot buy a platform banner. It can approximate one by asking volunteers to post 'I voted' and to message close friends on WhatsApp, which keeps the signal inside the bloc's own networks rather than on public feeds that NB voters also see. Expect tenths of a point per person reached.

findings.topic: Friend-tagging on Facebook (social pressure by peers)
findings.claim: In three experiments, volunteers tagged members of their own Facebook networks in status updates encouraging them to vote. Tags that revealed whether the person had voted in past elections produced substantial turnout increases, which the author reports as larger than typical face-to-face effects. Secondary coverage reports that a civic-duty tag alone did not raise turnout, and that 'social pressure by proxy' (telling people that they and many friends had voted) was not significant.
findings.quant: Effect sizes not extracted from the article. Secondary coverage gives the first experiment as 293 registered voters in Dallas County in the 2014 general election. The samples are small.
findings.authors: Katherine Haenschen
findings.title: Social Pressure on Social Media: Using Facebook Status Updates to Increase Voter Turnout
findings.relevance: Peer-delivered accountability is the legal Israeli substitute for vote-history mail. It is a friend who knows whether you voted, not a database. Public tagging is visible to opponents, so the change bloc should use private one-to-one or family-group messages. Small samples make this direction-only evidence.

findings.topic: Paid digital advertising at campaign scale
findings.claim: A pro-Biden group randomised its entire 8-month social-media persuasion programme ($8.9M) across 2 million moderate, low-information voters in five battleground states in 2020. The programme had no average effect on turnout. It slightly raised turnout among Biden leaners and slightly lowered it among Trump leaners, a small differential mobilisation that was strongest in early voting (exploratory).
findings.quant: Average turnout effect about 0. Biden leaners +0.4 pp (s.e. 0.2); Trump leaners -0.3 pp (s.e. 0.3); difference 0.7 pp (p = 0.036). US$8.9M; about 2 million voters; 5 states; 8 months.
findings.authors: Minali Aggarwal; Jennifer Allen; Alexander Coppock; Dan Frankowski; Solomon Messing; Kelly Zhang; James Barnes; Andrew Beasley; Harry Hantman; Sylvan Zheng
findings.title: A 2 million-person, campaign-wide field experiment shows how digital advertising affects voter turnout
findings.relevance: Paid social is not a turnout tool. At best it separates the two sides' leaners by tenths of a point. Narrowly targeted ads are low-visibility, so they carry little counter-mobilisation risk. Do not budget them as GOTV. Consistent with D3-F11.

findings.topic: Relational 'captain' model (supervised friend-to-friend)
findings.claim: Before November 2019 municipal elections, 43 volunteer 'captains' in four US states each proposed about 20 friends, relatives or neighbours. Half of each list was randomly assigned for the captain to mobilise, often repeatedly and in person or by phone. The other half was left alone as a control. Turnout in the target lists was far higher, with the largest effect under close organiser supervision (Ohio). The authors call it the largest intent-to-treat effect in two decades of GOTV experiments but stress that it is a low-salience pilot.
findings.quant: ITT +13.2 pp (s.e. 3.2), N = 773 (387 treated, 386 control); control turnout 32%. Ohio, highly supervised: +17.1 pp (s.e. 4.7). Other sites: +9.5 pp (s.e. 4.5). Difference in supervision 7.6 pp (s.e. 6.5), n.s.
findings.authors: Donald P. Green; Oliver A. McClellan
findings.title: Turnout Nation: A Pilot Experiment Evaluating a Get-Out-The-Vote 'Supertreatment'
findings.relevance: This is the best available design for scaling personal contact without public visibility. Israel's dense WhatsApp family and friend networks make it cheap. Each change-bloc volunteer owns about 10 named, likely-supportive friends, and an organiser checks in daily during the last 10 days (consistent with D3-F12's Outvote estimate). Discount heavily: control turnout here was 32%, while change supporters in strongholds turn out at about 75-80% (D5-F09), and effects shrink with salience (D3-F01). Captains should target their least-regular-voting friends.

findings.topic: Perceived closeness does not move individual turnout
findings.claim: Two field experiments in US gubernatorial elections showed voters a poll indicating either a close or a not-close race. Voters updated their beliefs about closeness, though they systematically overestimated the chance of a very close result. Their decision to vote was unaffected. A much larger 2014 postcard replication also found no turnout difference between close-poll and not-close-poll messages.
findings.quant: 2010: about 5,400 per arm. 2014: postcards to about 80,000 households (about 125,000 people), total sample over 1.38 million. The close-vs-not-close effect is ruled out above +0.8 pp, and perceptions explain at most 13% of the observed closeness-turnout relationship.
findings.authors: Alan Gerber; Mitchell Hoffman; John Morgan; Collin Raymond
findings.title: One in a Million: Field Experiments on Perceived Closeness of the Election and Voter Turnout
findings.relevance: A 'this race is close' message is not a GOTV treatment by itself. The value of closeness lies in how elites, media and organisers react to it (D11-F12), and that reaction is available to the NB as much as to the change bloc.

findings.topic: Pivotality message after a tied election
findings.claim: After a real tied election for a Massachusetts state legislative seat (as described in secondary sources), a large field experiment told voters that the rerun would be close. The message did little to raise turnout, and any effect was confined to a small group of frequent voters.
findings.quant: Overall effect about null (magnitudes not extracted).
findings.authors: Ryan D. Enos; Anthony Fowler
findings.title: Pivotality and Turnout: Evidence from a Field Experiment in the Aftermath of a Tied Election
findings.relevance: Even vivid proof that one vote can decide (Meretz missed the threshold by about 4,000 votes in 2022; P-F28) is a weak mobiliser for low-propensity voters. Use it to recruit and motivate volunteers, not as mass GOTV copy.

findings.topic: Published close polls raise turnout, mostly for the underdog
findings.claim: The authors used the exact release dates of Swiss national polls on high-stakes federal referenda and daily mail-in voting data from Geneva. Turnout rose sharply right after a closer poll was released, with no pre-release differences. The effect was largest where newspapers covered polls most, and it was asymmetric, raising the trailing side's vote share. The authors estimate it is large enough to flip close outcomes.
findings.quant: A one-SD (7.65-pt) closer poll raises turnout by about 0.4 pp a day for three days, about 1.2 pp in total. This matches the observational rule of thumb that 10 pts closer means 1-2 pp more turnout. Effects were larger in politically unrepresentative municipalities.
findings.authors: Leonardo Bursztyn; Davide Cantoni; Patricia Funk; Felix Schoenenberger; Noam Yuchtman
findings.title: Identifying the Effect of Election Closeness on Voter Turnout: Evidence from Swiss Referenda
findings.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 22(2): 876-914
findings.relevance: In aggregate, closeness amplified by the media mobilises the side that sees itself as trailing. Neither bloc is at 61 in 2026, so both can claim to be the underdog. Change-bloc triumphalism ('Netanyahu is finished') hands that role to the NB. 'Decided by a few thousand votes' is accurate and keeps the motivation on the change side.

findings.topic: Knowing the likely outcome demobilises (natural experiment)
findings.claim: Before a French voting reform, voters in some overseas territories cast ballots after mainland exit-poll results were already public. Comparing the same constituencies with and without that information, knowing the exit polls reduced turnout and increased bandwagon voting: those who still voted were more likely to back the expected winner.
findings.quant: Turnout about -11 pp when exit-poll information was known; bandwagon voting significantly higher (magnitude not extracted).
findings.authors: Rebecca B. Morton; Daniel Muller; Lionel Page; Benno Torgler
findings.title: Exit polls, turnout, and bandwagon voting: Evidence from a natural experiment
findings.relevance: Israel bans new polls in the final days (D11-F14) and exit polls appear only at 22:00. The live analogue in 2026 is the Central Elections Committee's polling-station turnout releases on election day (D5-F26) and parties' claims that the race is decided. 'It's in the bag' messages depress the turnout of whichever side believes them.

findings.topic: Israel's pre-election poll blackout (law)
findings.claim: Section 16(h) of the Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law forbids broadcasting or publishing the results of any election poll not already published, from the end of the Friday before polling day until the polls close. Anyone re-publishing an earlier poll in that window must state prominently that it is not current and says nothing about voters' views on the day. Poll publishers must also file methodology and sample details with the Central Elections Committee and report sponsors to the State Comptroller.
findings.quant: 2026 blackout: from the end of Friday 23 October to the close of polls on Tuesday 27 October (22:00 at most stations; D2-F17), about four days. Comparative: France one week, Spain five days, Italy 15 days, and no restriction in the US, UK, Germany or Netherlands (IDI comparative table, 2002).
findings.authors: Knesset; text as published by the Central Elections Committee (ref. 2022-000238)
findings.title: Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959, section 16 (election polls)
findings.relevance: The final published polls (Friday 23 October) fix expectations for four days. Parties' internal 'polls' and alarm messages fill the gap, which is the window in which Likud's 2015 late surge happened (D11-F30, P-F30). Plan the last-weekend message on the assumption that the NB will claim it is losing.

findings.topic: Probabilistic forecasts inflate certainty and can demobilise
findings.claim: In experiments, people shown win probabilities, rather than vote-share projections, were more likely to confuse the two and to see the leader as more decisively ahead. In an incentivised voting game, participants voted less when forecasts showed higher odds for one side, but did not respond to changes in vote share. ANES data show that people expecting a lopsided race were less likely to report voting. The authors cannot say whether forecasts mattered in 2016.
findings.quant: 8.6% confused vote share with probability after seeing probabilistic forecasts, vs 0.6% after vote-share projections. Expecting a lopsided race was associated with about 3 pp lower reported turnout (observational ANES). Effects concentrated among supporters of the leading candidate. These figures are from the authors' published response to critics; the article itself was not accessed.
findings.authors: Sean J. Westwood; Solomon Messing; Yphtach Lelkes
findings.title: Projecting Confidence: How the Probabilistic Horse Race Confuses and Demobilizes the Public
findings.relevance: The Knesset Model publishes probabilities (P(change-led government) about 18.5%, repeat election about 42%). Bloc communications should translate these into seats and votes-to-61 (for example, 'about 30,000 votes decided 2022') and never into 'chance of winning'.

findings.topic: Lab evidence: polls can boost the expected majority's turnout
findings.claim: Laboratory voting experiments found that participation was higher among people who expected their side to win by a larger margin. Releasing pre-election polls raised the expected majority's turnout and produced more lopsided results, the opposite of the underdog pattern in the Swiss field data.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted (lab study).
findings.authors: Marina Agranov; Jacob K. Goeree; Julian Romero; Leeat Yariv
findings.title: What Makes Voters Turn Out: The Effects of Polls and Beliefs
findings.venue: Journal of the European Economic Association 16(3): 825-856
findings.relevance: Whether published polls create an underdog or a bandwagon turnout response is not settled. Compare D11-F12 (field, underdog) with this study (lab, bandwagon). The model should not hard-code either direction, and the bloc should not stake its message on one.

findings.topic: Bandwagon effects on vote intention (multiparty, Denmark)
findings.claim: In a Danish national survey experiment, respondents read a news story showing either a large governing party or a small opposition party gaining or losing in the polls. Their vote intentions moved in the direction shown. The effect was stronger for gains than for losses, held for both parties, and did not vary across socio-demographic groups.
findings.quant: YouGov panel, January 2014, 3,011 complete responses, five arms. Social Democrats shown moving +/-5 pp, Conservatives +/-2 pp. Gain vs loss: p < 0.05 for both parties. Gain vs control (joint test): p < 0.05. Loss vs control: negative, n.s.
findings.authors: Jens Olav Dahlgaard; Jonas Hedegaard Hansen; Kasper M. Hansen; Martin V. Larsen
findings.title: How Election Polls Shape Voting Behaviour
findings.relevance: Momentum coverage reallocates votes, mainly within blocs (Yashar vs Together vs Democrats), which adds nothing to bloc seats. It can also speed desertion from Blue and White, which is polling below the threshold, and that does add to the bloc (P-F25). Reservists deserters split partly toward Likud, so rescuing them hurts the deny-61 objective (MODEL_BRIEF_v2). Use 'momentum' framing only to rescue Blue and White votes, not to fight within the bloc or to target Reservists voters.

findings.topic: Bandwagon effects are subtle and not concentrated among undecideds (Netherlands)
findings.claim: In a survey experiment with a large cross-section of Dutch voters using real poll results, simply showing poll standings had no effect on later vote intentions. Stressing that a party was growing produced a small bandwagon effect. That effect was not larger among undecided voters.
findings.quant: N = 23,421. Plain poll standings: no effect. Growth framing: small positive effect. No moderation by indecision.
findings.authors: Tom W.G. van der Meer; Armen Hakhverdian; Loes Aaldering
findings.title: Off the Fence, Onto the Bandwagon? A Large-Scale Survey Experiment on Effect of Real-Life Poll Outcomes on Subsequent Vote Intentions
findings.venue: International Journal of Public Opinion Research 28(1): 46-72
findings.relevance: Poll framing in the last fortnight is a weak lever on the roughly 1% of voters torn between blocs (D5-F08). Do not expect momentum messaging to reach the undecided.

findings.topic: Negative partisanship drives turnout in PR systems
findings.claim: Using CSES Module 3 data from 17 European multiparty PR systems, the study finds that holding a negative party identity (strong dislike of a party) raises turnout independently of positive partisanship. Its effect on vote choice is smaller and not uniform across party families.
findings.quant: Turnout about +9 pp for negative partisans; vote-choice effect about 2-6 pp; 17 PR systems.
findings.authors: Sabrina Jasmin Mayer
findings.title: How negative partisanship affects voting behavior in Europe: Evidence from an analysis of 17 European multi-party systems with proportional voting
findings.relevance: Anti-Netanyahu sentiment is the change bloc's most reliable turnout engine. Hostility toward 'the left', Arab parties and the protest movement does the same for the NB. Israel's bloc structure is built on this kind of dislike (D1-F04, D1-F06).

findings.topic: Affective polarisation raises turnout, including among less sophisticated voters
findings.claim: Combining three decades of German cross-sections, a Spanish two-wave panel and an 11-wave Dutch panel, the study finds that affective polarisation has a sizeable independent effect on turnout. The effect holds after addressing reverse causality and controlling for positive partisanship and ideological polarisation. It may be somewhat stronger among the least politically sophisticated.
findings.quant: No single magnitude extracted; described as a 'sizeable independent effect'.
findings.authors: Eelco Harteveld; Markus Wagner
findings.title: Does affective polarisation increase turnout? Evidence from Germany, The Netherlands and Spain
findings.relevance: Israel's affective polarisation is at a record level (6.2 in 2022; D1-F04) and has not fallen since October 7 (D1-F05). The salience of electoral competition raises it further (P-F15). A more polarised final fortnight raises turnout on both sides, and the effect may be strongest among low-sophistication voters. Those voters are concentrated in the NB's low-turnout reservoir (D5-F16), so the bloc is hurt if the campaign turns into a tribal showdown.

findings.topic: Anger mobilises more than anxiety or enthusiasm
findings.claim: Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, the authors predicted and found that anger, more than anxiety or enthusiasm, drives political participation. Support comes from a randomised experiment, a national survey of the 2008 US electorate, and pooled ANES data from 1980 to 2004.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted.
findings.authors: Nicholas A. Valentino; Ted Brader; Eric W. Groenendyk; Krysha Gregorowicz; Vincent L. Hutchings
findings.title: Election Night's Alright for Fighting: The Role of Emotions in Political Participation
findings.relevance: Anger over October 7 accountability and the draft (D5-F21, D5-F11) is mobilising fuel for change voters. Delivered through broadcast media to the whole electorate, the same anger cues give NB voters someone to be angry at. Aim anger at the government's record, not at NB voters' communities.

findings.topic: Negative campaigning does not depress turnout (meta-analysis)
findings.claim: A meta-analysis of 111 studies found no reliable evidence that negative campaigning depresses turnout. It does slightly lower political efficacy and trust. There is tentative support for the idea that negativity stimulates partisans but turns off independents.
findings.quant: 111 studies, 57 with turnout outcomes. Overall turnout effect: no reliable demobilisation. Partisans-vs-independents test based on only 9 studies, not significant.
findings.authors: Richard R. Lau; Lee Sigelman; Ivy Brown Rovner
findings.title: The Effects of Negative Political Campaigns: A Meta-Analytic Reassessment
findings.relevance: Contrast messaging is not a turnout risk for the change bloc's own base. The risk lies in who sees it. If negativity stimulates partisans on both sides, broadcast attacks energise NB partisans as well.

findings.topic: When negativity demobilises
findings.claim: Using the 2004 US presidential campaign and elections from 1976 to 2000, the study shows that negative information lowers turnout only when two conditions hold: the voter has already chosen a candidate, and the negativity is about that chosen candidate. Otherwise negativity does not demobilise and can mobilise.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted.
findings.authors: Yanna Krupnikov
findings.title: When Does Negativity Demobilize? Tracing the Conditional Effect of Negative Campaigning on Voter Turnout
findings.relevance: Late, credible, specific information about Likud's record on October 7, the draft and the cost of living, reaching soft 2022 Likud voters who have decided but are disaffected (only 58% definite; D5-F11), can lower their turnout without persuading them to switch. It should go through targeted, low-visibility channels and peer messengers (P-F14), not through broadcast attacks that rally the whole NB.

findings.topic: Message tone and partisans' turnout
findings.claim: Field experiments in two US local elections sent candidates' partisans negative or positive letters. Negative letters produced significantly higher partisan turnout than positive ones, mainly because positive letters lowered turnout relative to no letter. Separately, Arceneaux and Nickerson (2010, American Politics Research 38(1): 54-83, doi:10.1177/1532673X09331613) found no systematic difference between negative and positive personal-contact scripts in two 2004 experiments with about 69,000 people contacted.
findings.quant: Negative vs positive: higher turnout among partisans (magnitude not extracted). Negative vs control: no significant difference. Positive vs control: lower turnout.
findings.authors: Jared Barton; Marco Castillo; Ragan Petrie
findings.title: Negative campaigning, fundraising, and voter turnout: A field experiment
findings.relevance: For the bloc's own supporters, a 'what is at stake' contrast frame is at least as mobilising as an upbeat one. Purely feel-good GOTV copy may underperform. The variable that matters for counter-mobilisation is who sees the message, not its tone.

findings.topic: Threat framing motivates activists and donors
findings.claim: A lobbying organisation randomised three versions of a letter to its constituents: one stressing threatened, unwanted policy changes, one stressing opportunities, and a control. The threat letter increased the number of financial contributions, and the opportunity letter increased the number of signed postcards to the president.
findings.quant: Magnitudes not extracted.
findings.authors: Joanne M. Miller; Jon A. Krosnick
findings.title: Threat as a Motivator of Political Activism: A Field Experiment
findings.relevance: 'What we lose if the NB reaches 61' is the right frame for recruiting relational captains and donors, delivered inside closed supporter channels. The same threat frame spread publicly about NB communities is the trigger for counter-mobilisation (D11-F27).

findings.topic: Persuasion contact can backfire
findings.claim: A field experiment with about 56,000 Wisconsin voters in the 2008 presidential election tested persuasion canvassing, phone calls and mail. The appeals possibly reduced support for the candidate and almost certainly did not increase it. Persuasive canvassing also reduced response to a follow-up survey among infrequent voters. The authors conclude that campaign contact can provoke a backlash.
findings.quant: N about 56,000. Candidate-support effect: possibly negative and not positive (magnitude not extracted).
findings.authors: Michael A. Bailey; Daniel J. Hopkins; Todd Rogers
findings.title: Unresponsive and Unpersuaded: The Unintended Consequences of a Voter Persuasion Effort
findings.relevance: Door contact with NB-leaning households is not costless. The atlas already restricts door work to turf where its value is positive and keeps out of NB-majority turf (MODEL_BRIEF_v2). This finding supports that rule, and shows that in NB turf the change bloc should rely on calls to identified soft voters, not door-to-door persuasion (consistent with P-F01, P-F14).

findings.topic: Israel 2019: suppression campaign and Arab counter-mobilisation
findings.claim: In April 2019 Likud-affiliated representatives carried about 1,200 hidden cameras into polling stations in Arab towns, and an organiser later boasted on Facebook that this had pushed Arab turnout below 50%. Likud then pushed a camera bill and warned about Arab turnout ahead of the September rerun. In September, Arab-list votes jumped far faster than total votes, and a Likud MK said the camera bill had 'woken up' the Arab sector. The rise is confounded by the reunification of the Joint List between the two elections.
findings.quant: Official CEC totals: Arab lists 337,108 (Apr 2019, two lists) to 470,211 (Sep 2019, Joint List), +39.5%. All votes 4,340,253 to 4,465,168, +2.9%. Likud plus Kulanu 1,293,126 to Likud (merged) 1,113,617, -13.9%. Arab turnout 49.2% to about 59-60% (reported). Desk calculation from CEC locality files for the 21st and 22nd Knesset.
findings.authors: Desk 11 calculation from Central Elections Committee results; context from The Times of Israel (R. Ahren, 9 Apr 2019; J. Magid, 13 Aug 2019; ToI staff, 18 Sep 2019)
findings.title: Official results, 21st and 22nd Knesset; 'Arab turnout rises to 60% after reaching an all-time low in April'
findings.venue: Central Elections Committee; The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: This is the clearest Israeli case of a visible campaign against a group's turnout mobilising that group, a mirror image of the risk the change bloc faces. Content that Haredi, settler or Mizrahi-periphery voters experience as an attempt to exclude, ridicule or 'out-vote' them carries the same risk. Extends D3-F32, D2-F24 and D6-F25 with official vote counts.

findings.topic: Israel 2019-20: Likud's demonstrated mobilisation capacity
findings.claim: Between the September 2019 and March 2020 elections, Likud gained more votes than any other list. Total votes rose much less, and the decline of Yamina and Otzma Yehudit can account for only about a third of Likud's gain. The rest came from new or returning voters and from other lists, concentrated in Likud's peripheral and southern strongholds (D6-F05). The Joint List also grew strongly in the same election.
findings.quant: Official CEC totals: Likud 1,113,617 to 1,352,449 (+238,832; +21.4%). Yamina plus Otzma down 84,173. Total votes +149,967 (+3.4%). Joint List +111,296 (+23.7%). Blue and White +69,167. Desk calculation from CEC locality files for the 22nd and 23rd Knesset.
findings.authors: Desk 11 calculation from Central Elections Committee results
findings.title: Official results, 22nd and 23rd Knesset (locality files)
findings.relevance: Likud can add 150,000-240,000 votes within five months when it frames an election as existential and targets stronghold non-voters. The 2026 'Golden Clusters' goal of 200,000 extra voters (D5-F17) is within this historical range, not fantasy. This is the reservoir the change bloc must avoid activating.

findings.topic: Israel 2021-22: differential mobilisation by bloc
findings.claim: From 2021 to 2022, total votes rose 8.1%. The Haredi lists grew more than twice as fast and the right-wing lists roughly matched the overall rise, while the combined change-camp lists slightly lost votes. Arab-list votes rose sharply from a record-low base. This differential, not vote switching, is what turned a near-tie into a 64-seat majority, together with the 4,000-vote Meretz threshold miss (P-F28, D1-F12).
findings.quant: Official CEC totals including envelopes. Haredi lists (Shas, UTJ) 564,399 to 673,158, +19.3%. Right lists (Likud, RZP or RZP-Otzma, Yamina or Jewish Home) 1,566,369 to 1,688,581, +7.8%. Change-camp lists (Yesh Atid, Blue and White or National Unity, New Hope, Labor, Meretz, YB) 1,834,885 to 1,820,389, -0.8%. Arab lists 379,647 to 511,399, +34.7%. All votes 4,436,365 to 4,794,593, +8.1%. The same pattern was reported by Davies and Hantman (Times of Israel, 7 Nov 2022), who add that Haredi parties polled 15 seats but won 18.
findings.authors: Desk 11 calculation from Central Elections Committee results (expc_24, expc_25)
findings.title: Official results, 24th and 25th Knesset (locality files)
findings.relevance: In the last comparable cycle, the NB's sectoral machines (Haredi most of all) out-mobilised the change camp by about 20 points of vote growth. The change bloc's 2026 enthusiasm edge (D6-F38) reverses the survey picture but not the machinery. Model a Haredi plus right-wing surge scenario explicitly.

findings.topic: Israel 2015: blackout, late deciders and an election-day surge
findings.claim: Commentary written the day after the 2015 election noted that the legal ban on polls in the closing days meant pollsters missed a late Likud surge, and that even exit polls were wrong. It added that a late surge visible in exit-poll data suggested Netanyahu's 'us or them' panic campaign produced real results, especially late on election day. A post-election survey reported that 28% of voters decided just before the election. No causal estimate of the election-day 'Arabs in droves' message exists (D3-F33).
findings.quant: Final published polls had Likud at 20-23 seats; result 30 (P-F30). Post-election survey of 1,133 voters: 28% decided just ahead of the election (Jerusalem Post, 20 Apr 2015; sponsor not given on the retrieved page).
findings.authors: William A. Galston; Yishai Schwartz (Brookings); Gil Hoffman (Jerusalem Post)
findings.title: Israel's election: What happened? (18 Mar 2015); 'Study finds 28 percent decided how to vote just ahead of election' (20 Apr 2015)
findings.relevance: The blackout window (D11-F14) plus election-day alarm calls is Likud's proven late-mobilisation format. In 2026 it will be fed by the CEC's polling-station turnout releases (D5-F26, D5-F27). The change bloc should pre-commit to answering through its own networks and should not supply 'left is surging' material.

findings.topic: Haredi and national-religious vote cohesion
findings.claim: Pooled IDI surveys from after the 2022 election show that Haredi voters remain highly cohesive behind the Haredi lists, with small leakage to RZP-Otzma and Likud. National-religious voters consolidated sharply behind RZP-Otzma. Both sectors are close to their turnout ceiling (D2-F12, D2-F04), so their swing capacity lies in whether they turn out at all, not in vote choice.
findings.quant: Haredim, 2022 (2021): Haredi lists 86% (89%), of which UTJ 58% and Shas 28%; RZP-Otzma 7% (4%); Likud 4%. National-religious, 2022 (2021): RZP-Otzma 45% (30%); Likud about 22.5% (about 23%); Haredi lists 13% (11%). 20 surveys, 10,694 Jewish voters, Nov 2022-Oct 2023.
findings.authors: Ariel Finkelstein (Israel Democracy Institute, Viterbi Family Center)
findings.title: Voting Patterns of Jews in the 2022 Elections by Religious Self-Definition
findings.relevance: Because Haredi vote choice is nearly fixed, a 1-point change in Haredi-sector turnout is worth about 3,150 net NB votes (D11-F34). It is the single most leveraged turnout variable on the NB side, and the change bloc cannot raise it, only fail to provoke it. Complements D1-F14 and D1-F20.

findings.topic: Haredi turnout in 2026: abstention payments and rabbinic counter-pressure
findings.claim: On Friday 25 September 2026, CEC chair Justice Noam Sohlberg issued an injunction barring the Satmar-linked charity 'Shekel HaTahor' from giving, offering or promising money to voters to stay home. The Movement for Quality Government had petitioned, alleging payments of $200 to Hasidim who pledged not to vote; the injunction remains until further notice and law enforcement is examining the group's finances. Rabbi Dov Lando, spiritual leader of Degel HaTorah, called campaigns urging Haredim to abstain a 'great crime'. Separately, ToI reported in August that about 7,000 of Likud's roughly 140,000 members are Haredi, some of whom said they would vote UTJ or Shas.
findings.quant: Alleged payment $200 per pledge (petitioner's claim, not a court finding). No estimate of the number of abstainers is available. The UTJ chair privately fears a drop in turnout (D5-F24).
findings.authors: Hezki Baruch (Israel National News); Shilo Freid (Ynet); Sam Sokol (Times of Israel)
findings.title: 'Sohlberg blocks Satmar hasidic group' (25 Sep 2026); 'Top rabbi calls Haredi election boycott a great crime'; 'Haredi turnout high in Likud primary...' (18 Aug 2026)
findings.venue: Israel National News; Ynetnews; The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: Haredi turnout is the NB's least certain flank in 2026. The leadership is already working to raise it. A change-bloc campaign that makes the draft a public battle cry aimed at Haredim gives rabbis the external threat that mobilises best (D11-F21, D11-F27). Keep the draft argument in secular and traditional channels.

findings.topic: Visible opposition mobilisation becomes a Likud mobilisation narrative and a legal target
findings.claim: A bipartisan US Senate staff report found that OneVoice, after its State Department grants ended in November 2014, redeployed the campaign infrastructure it had built partly with grant funds to V15, a campaign to defeat the incumbent Israeli government in 2015. Likud filed complaints with the Central Elections Committee at the time and framed the effort as a foreign plot to topple it. The pattern has repeated: Likud fought the Zazim buses in 2019 (D2-F10, D6-F23) and petitioned against the Fly&Vote expat flights in 2026. The 2026 case ended on 6 October in a compromise: no ticket subsidies, no flights beyond the six already advertised, and NIS 10,000 toward Likud's legal costs.
findings.quant: 2026: AID Coalition says about 53,000 Israelis plan to fly in to vote (organisation's claim; ToI, 7 Oct 2026); six flights; NIS 10,000 legal costs. 2015: the report criticised State Department oversight; it did not find that grant funds were spent directly on the election campaign.
findings.authors: U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (Rob Portman, chair; Claire McCaskill, ranking member); The Times of Israel staff (7 Oct 2026)
findings.title: Review of U.S. State Department Grants to OneVoice (staff report, 12 July 2016); 'Likud inks compromise with Israeli expat voter effort; 53,000 said planning to fly in for election'
findings.venue: U.S. Senate; The Times of Israel
findings.relevance: Every organised, visible, externally funded or transport-heavy pro-change turnout effort hands Likud a 'they are stealing the election' story and a court case. The 2026 rules are tight: no benefits of monetary value, no anonymous messages (CEC 2019), and payments to abstain are criminal (D11-F32). Keep the field operation decentralised, volunteer-run and cleared by counsel, and do not promote the expat flights in Israeli media.

findings.topic: The arithmetic of counter-mobilisation (desk calculation)
findings.claim: Using the atlas segment table (2022 eligible voters by segment and 2026 projected bloc shares), a 1-point turnout rise across NB-leaning segments nets far more votes for the NB than the same rise across change-leaning Jewish segments nets for the change bloc. A uniform national turnout rise, or a uniform rise across Jewish segments, also favours the NB. So 'raise national turnout' is the wrong objective, and even a small counter-mobilisation cancels a realistic change-bloc field programme.
findings.quant: Per 1 pp turnout rise: NB-leaning segments (Haredi, Jerusalem, Likud-leaning periphery, Russian-speaking, religious-Zionist, settlements, mixed cities; 3.12M eligible) about +10,770 net NB votes. Change-leaning Jewish segments (liberal urban, kibbutz, moshav, mixed urban; 2.73M eligible) about +6,760 net change votes. Uniform national rise +3,130 NB; uniform Jewish-sector rise +4,010 NB. Haredi sector alone +3,160 NB; periphery plus Haredi +5,940 NB. Realistic change-bloc programmes yield 745-2,046 net vote-equivalents (MODEL_BRIEF_v2), so break-even NB counter-mobilisation is 0.07-0.19 pp across NB segments, or 0.13-0.34 pp in periphery plus Haredi alone.
findings.authors: Desk 11 calculation from The Knesset Model atlas (segments.csv: CEC 2022 locality results, CBS classifications, 10 Oct 2026 forecast shares)
findings.title: Break-even counter-mobilisation for change-bloc field programmes
findings.relevance: This turns the qualitative backlash literature into a budget rule. Any tactic whose visibility could raise NB-segment turnout by even a tenth of a point must be expected to deliver more than about 1,000 net change votes, or be dropped. Assumptions: marginal voters vote like their segment's average (marginal NB-periphery voters are probably more right-leaning; see D1-F15), 2022 rolls include voters abroad, and raw net votes are treated as comparable to the atlas's vote-equivalents.

open_questions: No randomised GOTV or counter-mobilisation experiment from an Israeli Knesset election was found. All per-contact numbers are imported. Can the change bloc randomise relational captain lists (half of each captain's names held back until after the election) and measure the result from post-election self-reports, given that official individual turnout records are unavailable?

Is there any lawful Israeli source of individual vote history, for example a voter's own recollection gathered by a friend? If not, vote-history social pressure (D11-F01, D11-F02) is off the table, and Israeli campaigns should be told so explicitly.

No causal estimate exists for the 2015 'droves' message or for the 2019 cameras separate from the Joint List merger (D11-F27, D11-F30, D3-F33). Polling-station-level hourly turnout from earlier elections is not public. The CEC's four intraday station releases in 2026 (D5-F26) will for the first time allow measuring how quickly NB strongholds respond to visible change-bloc surges. Who will capture and analyse them on the day?

Which bloc will Israeli voters see as the underdog in the final week? The Swiss field evidence (underdog; D11-F12) and lab evidence (bandwagon; D11-F16) conflict, and Israeli coalition-minded voting (P-F26, P-F27) may produce either.

Does the Knesset Model's own publication of win probabilities affect turnout (D11-F15)? An A/B test of seat-based vs probability-based presentation among supporters could check stated motivation before 23 October.

How large is the Haredi abstention risk (Satmar-linked payments, draft anger, the new Haredi Public list)? No 2026 Haredi turnout-intention poll was found. A sector-specific poll would sharpen the most leveraged NB-side parameter (D11-F31, D11-F32, D11-F34).

The desk calculation (D11-F34) assumes marginal voters vote like their segment's average. Marginal low-propensity voters in periphery and Russian-speaking segments may lean further right (D1-F15). Re-estimating with polling-station turnout-propensity strata would refine the break-even.

Search budget ran out before these could be verified: Panagopoulos (2011) gratitude ('thank you for voting') mailers; Mann (2010) and Matland & Murray (2013) on social-pressure backlash complaints; Cox & Munger (1989) on elite mobilisation in close races; Delli Carpini (1984) and Jackson (1983) on early election-night calls; a 2018 Political Psychology online experiment on vote plans in Canada; Vote Rev's 2022 Georgia relational RCT figures; and the 'Vannetti' poll-effects study named in the brief, which could not be identified. Exact point estimates for Rogers et al. (2017), Gerber & Rogers (2009), Panagopoulos et al. (2014) and Haenschen (2016) were not extracted because the articles are paywalled.
